sentences: An unambiguous context-free grammar has at most one derivation tree for any particular word.
Its universality problem asks whether it generates every word over its alphabet.
The source places this decidable task between a polynomial-time lower bound and a polynomial-space upper bound and asks to tighten that gap.
Unambiguity removes duplicate derivations but still permits dependencies that a deterministic pushdown presentation cannot express.
Better bounds would measure how expensive exhaustive language coverage becomes when unique parsing replaces deterministic parsing as the structural promise.

cards.definitions: An automaton consists of a finite nonempty state set Q, a finite nonempty alphabet Σ, initial and final weight functions ι,τ:Q→ℤ∪{+∞}, and a transition weight δ:Q×Σ×Q→ℤ∪{+∞}. A weight +∞ marks an unavailable transition or endpoint. For w=a₁⋯a_m and a state sequence q₀,…,q_m, the run cost is ι(q₀)+Σ_{j=1}^m δ(q_{j−1},a_j,q_j)+τ(q_m), with +∞ absorbing under addition. Define A(w) as the minimum of these costs over all state sequences. For the empty word this is min_q(ι(q)+τ(q)); the minimum of no finite costs is +∞. There are no epsilon transitions, so each run consumes exactly one symbol per transition. Deterministic means that at most one state has finite initial weight and that for every state and input symbol at most one outgoing transition has finite weight. The candidate D may have different states, transitions and integer weights; equivalence requires D(w)=A(w), including agreement at +∞, for every w∈Σ*. Inputs explicitly list the finite sets and weight tables, using signed binary integers and a distinguished infinity symbol. The decision algorithm must terminate on every valid input, rejecting malformed encodings. The all-accepting and unweighted-endpoint presentation used in the main proof is linked to this endpoint-weighted presentation by Remark 8.1 and Appendix B of the cited full paper.
cards.answer_criterion: The original target requires decidability of this language of automata, or a proof of undecidability. It has been settled positively by the cited theorem. Decidability does not mean every weighted automaton is determinizable.

context_blocks.text: This historical question is resolved. Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald prove that an algorithm can decide whether a min-plus weighted automaton has an equivalent deterministic one. The result appeared as a 2025 preprint and at SODA 2026; a July 2026 follow-up gives a primitive-recursive upper bound on the decision complexity.

A weighted automaton reads a word and accumulates costs along each possible run. Min-plus semantics adds costs along a run, then chooses the smallest total among competing runs. This represents an optimal cost rather than only a yes/no acceptance answer.

For example, one branch can count the a symbols and another the b symbols. Taking the minimum computes min(#a,#b) for every word. Which branch gives the final minimum can change after a long suffix, and this function has no equivalent deterministic weighted automaton. The theorem decides when a deterministic equivalent exists; it does not say that one always does.

The ordinary Boolean subset construction only needs to remember which states remain possible. Here different ways of reaching a state may carry different integer costs. A finite set of original states therefore does not by itself give a finite set of quantitative configurations. This is why eliminating nondeterminism is a separate decision problem.

The 2022 source specifically left unrestricted ambiguity open after results for machines with only polynomially many runs. The later theorem covers the general case. Its model-variant discussion includes initial and final weights, so restricting the displayed proof to all-accepting automata does not leave the historical question unanswered.

The exact optimal running-time complexity is a different question. The 2025 decidability proof did not give a complexity bound, while the LICS 2026 result establishes a primitive-recursive one. This record retains its original decidability target and is hidden from the active reader as resolved.

cards.context:
This historical question is resolved. Almagor, Arbel and Sheinvald prove that an algorithm can decide whether a min-plus weighted automaton has an equivalent deterministic one. The result appeared as a 2025 preprint and at SODA 2026; a July 2026 follow-up gives a primitive-recursive upper bound on the decision complexity.

A weighted automaton reads a word and accumulates costs along each possible run. Min-plus semantics adds costs along a run, then chooses the smallest total among competing runs. This represents an optimal cost rather than only a yes/no acceptance answer.

For example, one branch can count the a symbols and another the b symbols. Taking the minimum computes min(#a,#b) for every word. Which branch gives the final minimum can change after a long suffix, and this function has no equivalent deterministic weighted automaton. The theorem decides when a deterministic equivalent exists; it does not say that one always does.

The ordinary Boolean subset construction only needs to remember which states remain possible. Here different ways of reaching a state may carry different integer costs. A finite set of original states therefore does not by itself give a finite set of quantitative configurations. This is why eliminating nondeterminism is a separate decision problem.

The 2022 source specifically left unrestricted ambiguity open after results for machines with only polynomially many runs. The later theorem covers the general case. Its model-variant discussion includes initial and final weights, so restricting the displayed proof to all-accepting automata does not leave the historical question unanswered.

The exact optimal running-time complexity is a different question. The 2025 decidability proof did not give a complexity bound, while the LICS 2026 result establishes a primitive-recursive one. This record retains its original decidability target and is hidden from the active reader as resolved.

methodology: Detailed cards have individually written statements, context, significance, and documented results. Source notes are unfinished research records and do not yet meet that standard. The legacy index is retained for traceability.
Open in the source means open at the date of that source. The build date, 10 September 2026, does not establish current open status. Old excerpts may omit conditions or subsequent results.

Selection considers model power, necessary resources, sharp bounds, structural characterizations, explicit constructions, and minimal assumptions. Source notes use a heuristic screen; detailed cards give an individual explanation.

The earlier automatic paper screen allowed at most one new card per paper title and rejected identical formulations and close duplicates within a source. Approved textbook and survey imports retain multiple distinct questions per publication. Confirmed overlaps supplement existing cards; collection-wide semantic deduplication remains incomplete.

Short quotations retain the source language. Later related literature, where listed, is a research aid rather than evidence of resolution. Personal notes and saved cards are stored locally in your browser.

Textbook and survey questions are dated paraphrases; source locations, conjectures, research directions and caveats are preserved on the problem cards. These annotations do not establish current open status or change a later card review. New source drafts remain unassessed for importance. The reader contains the imported questions and external bibliographic references only; source files are not bundled.

Selection groups follow the agreed 10 large and 25 small categories. We aim for benchmarks of 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. All three use the same category order and the same ranking within each category. The respective prefixes are 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 problems per large/small category. The possible 1,000-problem expansion has 1000 assigned places and 0 reserved places. Each card records its category explicitly. These counts describe saved candidates; classification does not verify a statement or its current open status. Deleted records are absent from the catalogue and exports. Their stable IDs and reasons are retained to prevent reimport. Final quota selection and a comprehensive deduplication audit remain pending.

Importance ordering is an editorial assessment of foundational significance, breadth of consequences, and influence on other questions. Each assessed card gives a reason. The category-wide review also uses shared priority bands for questions of comparable scope; it does not claim that these ties have a scientifically meaningful internal order. Unassessed drafts share a provisional score of 50; their relative order is only an ID tie-break, not an importance judgment. The first 5/2 places in each large/small category are an explicit editorial focus selection balancing importance and topical diversity. Focus ordering does not alter importance scores; remaining candidates use score and ID order. The targets are 100 and 500 problems, with a possible expansion to 1,000. Top 100, Top 500 and the possible Top 1000 use the first 5/2, 25/10 and 50/20 category places respectively, all from the same ranking. Category positions include all candidates and remain fixed when filtering. Publication date, source date, and card detail do not increase importance. Records marked resolved are placed after the remaining candidates, without changing their historical importance score. Importance review does not establish that a saved question is still open.
